input: The rate constant $k$ (s⁻¹) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, and the results are as follows. At 300 K, the rate constant was found to be $k$ = 0.056 s⁻¹. At 340 K, the corresponding value is $k$ = 2.555 s⁻¹, a figure that was not measured directly but was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 81 kJ mol⁻¹, and it should therefore be understood as a derived value rather than a measurement. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ amounted to 4%, which gives a useful indication of the repeatability of the measurements at each temperature. Because the reaction is first order, each value of $k$ summarises the decay of the reactant concentration over the measurement runs at that temperature, and the triplicate determinations stand behind each reported figure. The increase between the two temperatures is clearly very large, underlining the strong temperature sensitivity of the reaction over this interval. It is also important to note that above 340 K the solvent was observed to evaporate during sampling, which compromised the samples, and so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. Each determination was made on the reacting mixture as sampled at the stated temperature, and the reported constant belongs to that temperature alone. The reported range is therefore bounded by the sampling behaviour of the solvent rather than by the kinetics themselves, and any use of these values, including any comparison with rate constants obtained elsewhere, should respect that boundary and should also remember which of the two values was measured and which was derived.
target: The rate constant $k$ (s⁻¹) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.056 s⁻¹. At 340 K, $k$ = 2.555 s⁻¹; the higher value is derived, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 81 kJ mol⁻¹. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. Each reported value summarises the decay of the reactant concentration across its triplicate runs, the first-order form being what allows a single constant to carry the decay at a fixed temperature. The derived status of the higher value travels with it: a comparison against a measured rate constant at another temperature compares a measurement with a computation from the Arrhenius relation, and the computation inherits the relation's fit over the measured interval rather than adding a measurement at its own temperature. A first-order constant carries the whole decay at its temperature: the concentration falls by the same fraction in each equal interval of time, so the constant is a complete summary of the rate behaviour the triplicate runs observed, and the spread of the runs around it is what the relative standard deviation reports. The derived value extends the measured constant along the Arrhenius relation rather than adding a determination of its own, and its standing in any later use is that of a computed point on the fitted temperature dependence. The measurements and the derivation together fix the temperature dependence only across the interval the sampling allowed. Rate constants are bounded above by the sampling behaviour of the solvent. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K; the upper end of the range is set by that failure, not by the kinetics.
